lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You will hear two geography students, Callum and Priya, talking to their tutor about a fieldwork report. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Come in, both of you. So, I've read the draft of your river report. Before we get into my notes, remind me why you chose Holme Beck. It isn't the obvious place.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: No, people assume it's because it's near campus, but it's actually over an hour away by minibus.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: The main reason was that a group from three years ago did exactly the same measurements there. Their data's in the department archive, so we could compare our results with theirs.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: That's a good reason, and you should say so more clearly in the report. Was access straightforward?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Not at all. The farmer who owns the land took nearly three weeks to answer our letter. We'd almost given up.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Now, the introduction. I know you were worried about the length, but it's well under the word limit, so that isn't a problem. And the references are fine; you've used a good range.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: So what's wrong with it?

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: I read it twice and I still couldn't work out what you actually expected to find. There's no single sentence that says, for example, we predicted that the channel would get wider and the pebbles smaller as we moved downstream. That's your hypothesis, and it needs to be there in plain words.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Fair enough. That's easy to fix.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Good. Then there are the velocity measurements. I noticed you used floats rather than the flow meter.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Yes, we'd booked the department's flow meter, but when we went to collect it, it had already been lent to another group. So we timed oranges floating along a ten-metre stretch instead.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Oranges are perfectly respectable. Did they cause you any trouble?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: No, they worked really well, actually. The real problem was the weather. It poured with rain on the second night, and by the morning the river was about thirty centimetres higher. So the lower sites were measured in completely different conditions.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Ah, that explains the odd jump in your figures. And you still managed to visit all eight sites?

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Yes, just about. We finished with an hour to spare.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Right, let's go through the report section by section. First, the site description.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: We were thinking of adding some photographs to that part. We took loads.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Photos are nice, but they won't tell the reader where anything is, so I wouldn't bother adding more. What's really missing is a map showing the eight sampling points along the river.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: OK, I can draw one up from our survey sheets.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: Next, there's a whole page listing your equipment: tape measures, poles, even your boots. My first thought was that it could go in an appendix, but to be honest, it adds nothing. The equipment is obvious from the method. Just take it out.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: And the data tables? They take up about six pages in the middle.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: That's the problem: they break up your argument. Keep every one of them, because the examiners like to see the raw numbers, but put them at the back in an appendix and refer to them in the text.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: What about the sediment section? I wondered whether we should merge it with the velocity section, since they're both about how the river changes downstream.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: No, I'd keep those two apart; they answer different questions. My worry with the sediment section is that you give the results without saying how you got them. How did you choose which pebbles to measure? Someone else should be able to repeat what you did, so the method needs a lot more detail.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: And the risk assessment? Can we drop that?

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: No, that has to stay, because it's a requirement for all fieldwork reports. But it's three pages long at the moment. A short paragraph on the main hazards would be plenty, so cut it right down.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: This is a lot to do. The deadline's a week on Friday. Should we go back to Holme Beck and do the velocity readings again in dry weather?

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: I wouldn't. You won't get the minibus at such short notice, and the rain is part of the story anyway. What you should do instead is write a proper section on the limitations of your study: the rain, the floats, the small number of sites. Examiners respect honesty about what went wrong.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: OK, we'll definitely add that. I was also going to ask the lab technician to check our sediment weights again.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: There's no need. Sam already went through them with us last week.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Oh, of course. Fine.

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: One more thing: your graphs. The width graph and the depth graph use different scales along the bottom, so they look as if they disagree when they don't.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: That was my fault. I'll redo all of them with the same scale, starting from the source of the river.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: And should we get another group to read the report before we hand it in?

lines.speaker: tutor
lines.text: You could, but everyone's busy with their own reports now. I'd rather you read it aloud to each other. You'll catch most of the mistakes that way.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Right. Thanks, that's really helpful.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of the recording. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: Why did the students choose Holme Beck for their fieldwork?

options.text: It was close to the university.
Earlier data from the same site was available.
The landowner was quick to give permission.

explanation.correct: 'A group from three years ago did exactly the same measurements there' and their data is in the archive, so the students could compare results: earlier data from the same site was available.

distractors.why_wrong: Callum says people assume it is near campus, but it is over an hour away by minibus.
The farmer took nearly three weeks to answer their letter, so permission was slow.

evidence.quote: a group from three years ago did exactly the same measurements there

questions.prompt: What does the tutor say about the introduction to the report?

options.text: It is longer than allowed.
It does not state what the students predicted.
It has too few references.

explanation.correct: The tutor 'couldn't work out what you actually expected to find'; there is no sentence giving the hypothesis, i.e. what the students predicted.

distractors.why_wrong: It is 'well under the word limit', so length is not a problem.
The references are fine; they used 'a good range of sources'.

evidence.quote: I still couldn't work out what you actually expected to find

questions.prompt: What problem did the students have when measuring the speed of the river?

options.text: The flow meter stopped working.
The water level rose during the fieldwork.
They did not have time to visit every site.

explanation.correct: After heavy rain 'the river was about thirty centimetres higher', so the lower sites were measured in different conditions: the river level rose during the fieldwork.

distractors.why_wrong: The flow meter did not stop working: it had been lent to another group, and the oranges they used instead 'worked really well'.
They visited all eight sites and finished with an hour to spare.

evidence.quote: by the morning the river was about thirty centimetres higher
